topic: Undo/revert/rewind separation and safe recovery UX
research_questions: How do mature version-control, IDE, chat, and agent products distinguish undo, revert, rewind, checkpoint restore, and destructive recovery?
Which user-visible confirmations, previews, scopes, and recovery guarantees prevent accidental loss or ambiguous rollback?
How should Puppet Master represent operation identity, affected artifacts, provenance, reversibility, and partial failure across these recovery modes?
Which failure modes and accessibility or trust signals are documented by official or primary sources?

sources.title: Git - git-reset Documentation
sources.material_relevance: Defines reset as moving HEAD and optionally changing the index and worktree, with soft, mixed, hard, merge, keep, path-limited, and ORIG_HEAD recovery semantics.

sources.title: Git - git-revert Documentation
sources.material_relevance: Defines revert as recording new commits that reverse existing commits and documents clean-worktree, conflict, continue, skip, and abort behavior.

sources.title: Git - git-reflog Documentation
sources.material_relevance: Documents local reference logs, prior ref values, recovery breadcrumbs, and expiry or deletion limits on those breadcrumbs.

sources.title: User interface
sources.material_relevance: Documents Timeline and local file history with revision comparison, restore, deleted-file recovery, and configurable size, entry, exclusion, and merge-window limits.

sources.title: Revert changes with checkpoints and editing requests
sources.material_relevance: Separates editing a prior chat request from restoring a checkpoint, and documents confirmation, redo, file-change previews, and conversation forking.

sources.title: Local History
sources.material_relevance: Documents diff-driven full or selective restoration, deleted-file recovery, project or folder scope, labels, and explicit retention and size limits.

sources.title: Reverting a pull request
sources.material_relevance: Shows shared-history recovery as a new revert pull request with permissions, conflict handling, and a subsequent merge gate.

sources.title: Checkpointing
sources.material_relevance: Separates restore code, restore conversation, restore both, summarize, and fork; documents per-prompt checkpoints, persistence, retention, and coverage limits.

sources.title: Rewind file changes with checkpointing
sources.material_relevance: Defines checkpoint UUIDs, tracked edit tools, created and modified file restoration, code-only rewind, and non-capture of Bash changes.

sources.title: Microsoft Agent Framework Workflows - Checkpoints
sources.material_relevance: Provides checkpoint lifecycle and restore APIs, memory/file/distributed storage choices, durability implications, and trusted-storage security guidance.

sources.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2
sources.material_relevance: Defines error-prevention alternatives for data modification or deletion: reversible, checked, or confirmed, plus text identification of detected errors.

findings.claim: Git's public command model distinguishes additive revert from local reset: revert records new commits that reverse earlier commits, while reset moves HEAD and can alter the index and working tree according to mode.
findings.notes: The distinction is explicit in both manuals and is tied to different state scopes and history consequences.

findings.claim: Git reset exposes materially different safety scopes: soft leaves files and index, mixed updates the index, hard overwrites the worktree and may overwrite untracked files, while merge and keep can abort when local changes would be overwritten.
findings.notes: A generic reset button would hide meaningful loss and concurrency semantics that Git makes explicit through modes and pathspecs.

findings.claim: Git reflog provides local breadcrumbs for prior reference tips, but those entries can expire, be deleted, or be dropped and therefore are bounded recovery aids rather than permanent shared history.
findings.notes: The manual documents local ref updates, prior-value notation, and expiration of reachable and unreachable entries.

findings.claim: VS Code separates editing a previous chat request from restoring a checkpoint: editing reverts the original request and subsequent changes before resending, while checkpoint restore returns files to a selected conversation point without changing the prompts.
findings.notes: This gives users distinct controls for changing intent and for recovering a known-good workspace state.

findings.claim: VS Code checkpoint recovery includes confirmation, redo after an accidental restore, per-request file-change counts, and conversation forking from a checkpoint.
findings.notes: The documented flow makes target, scope, and alternative actions visible before and after recovery.

findings.claim: VS Code Timeline and JetBrains Local History make local recovery inspectable through revision lists and diffs, support full or selective restoration, and cover accidentally deleted files.
findings.notes: Both IDEs provide a reviewable history surface rather than requiring users to guess a target from a generic undo stack.

findings.claim: GitHub implements pull-request rollback as a new revert pull request, requiring write permission and a later merge; conflicts or non-GitHub fast-forward merges can require individual commit reverts.
findings.notes: The new change object preserves review and merge gates instead of silently rewriting a shared branch.

findings.claim: Claude Code exposes independent restore scopes for code, conversation, or both, while its summarize actions change context without changing files.
findings.notes: The product explicitly distinguishes artifact state from conversation state and offers a no-file-change summarization path.

findings.claim: Agent checkpoint coverage is tool- and session-bound: Claude tracks direct file-edit tools but not Bash or ordinary external concurrent edits; its SDK rewinds file state without rewinding conversation state, and checkpoint lifetime is limited or configurable.
findings.notes: Coverage and retention are part of the recovery contract and must not be implied to include every workspace side effect.

findings.claim: Microsoft Agent Framework models checkpoint durability through pluggable in-memory, file, and distributed storage and treats checkpoint storage as a trusted security boundary.
findings.notes: Storage choice changes restart and cross-process durability; authorization and tamper resistance are explicitly part of safe restore.

findings.claim: WCAG 2.2 frames safety for data modification or deletion as at least one of reversible, checked, or confirmed, and requires detected input errors to be identified and described in text.
findings.notes: The standard provides a useful confirmation and accessibility baseline for destructive recovery controls.

findings.claim: The reviewed systems imply that recovery scope is safer when encoded in a user-visible operation record than when inferred from a generic undo label.
findings.notes: This is a design inference from the documented differences among reset modes, chat checkpoints, and code-versus-conversation restore.

findings.claim: No reviewed source defines a universal transaction or atomicity guarantee for rewinding arbitrary shell commands, external systems, and concurrent actors together.
findings.notes: The reviewed documentation is explicit about file or workflow scope and non-captured changes, but does not provide a general cross-system rollback contract.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Layered recovery separates immediate edit undo or local history, session-level agent checkpoints, and durable shared-history version-control or pull-request reverts.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Use different recovery surfaces and guarantees for local edits, agent sessions, and shared history instead of one overloaded rollback action.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Recovery targets are anchored to user-visible history entries such as chat requests, prompt or checkpoint identifiers, local-history revisions, timestamps, commits, or refs, with diff or file-scope inspection available.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: A recovery target should be selectable and inspectable, not inferred from an opaque stack position.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Agent products distinguish artifact state from conversation state and offer code-only, conversation-only, both, or forked alternatives.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: A user can recover files without losing reasoning context, or branch an alternative without destroying the original session.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Shared-history rollback is additive: create an inverse commit or revert pull request, then apply normal review, permission, conflict, and merge gates.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Preserve provenance and collaboration controls for recovery that affects shared history.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Recovery workflows model partial failure with explicit continue, skip, abort, conflict, or retry paths rather than reporting a binary success only.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Recovery state should remain inspectable and resumable when the target cannot be applied cleanly.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Checkpoint boundaries align with meaningful user or workflow units: a chat request, a prompt, or a workflow superstep, with storage selected for intended durability.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Checkpoint granularity should follow meaningful operation boundaries and advertise whether it survives restart or distribution.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: Puppet Master should expose a common recovery envelope over these layers while preserving their different semantics and guarantees.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Unify metadata and previews, not the underlying meaning of undo, restore, rewind, revert, or reset.

competitor_standard_patterns.pattern: No reviewed source provides a cross-vendor standard vocabulary that guarantees users will interpret undo, revert, rewind, restore, and reset identically.
competitor_standard_patterns.implication: Treat labels as typed operation contracts with explanatory scope and consequence text rather than assuming synonymy.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A user selects destructive reset when they intended additive revert, causing uncommitted work to be overwritten or removed.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Use explicit operation names, scope previews, warnings for uncommitted or untracked loss, and a separate shared-history revert path.

failure_modes.failure_mode: Checkpoint restore appears complete while shell-command edits or concurrent manual edits remain outside the checkpoint coverage.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Show capture coverage per artifact and disclose non-captured commands, external edits, and concurrent session changes before confirmation.

failure_modes.failure_mode: The requested recovery target is unavailable because local-history, checkpoint, or reflog retention and size limits expired or pruned it.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Display retention and durability alongside each target, distinguish unavailable from empty, and offer durable version-control checkpoints for important states.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A shared-history revert encounters merge conflicts or cannot map to one merge commit, forcing manual commit-level recovery.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Expose conflict state and affected commits, keep the original change visible, and provide continue, abort, or smaller-scope recovery actions.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A user restores files but not the conversation, or rewinds conversation but keeps current files, and misinterprets what state was changed.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Use separate code and conversation scope controls and state the resulting state for each before and after recovery.

failure_modes.failure_mode: Checkpoint storage is tampered with, loaded from an untrusted source, or accessible to unauthorized actors.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Treat checkpoint storage as a trust boundary with authorization, integrity checks, provenance, and safe deserialization policy.

failure_modes.failure_mode: A broad rewind without an artifact-level preview erases unrelated changes made after the selected target.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Show the complete affected-artifact manifest, including additions, deletions, line changes, and non-captured edits, before applying the restore.

failure_modes.failure_mode: No reviewed source quantifies how often users choose the wrong recovery mode or target in real products.
failure_modes.mitigation_or_gap: Instrument mode and target selection, cancellation, conflict, and recovery-of-recovery outcomes; do not use an assumed error rate.

implications.implication: Puppet Master should treat shared-history reversion as a separate lifecycle from local checkpoint or artifact restoration because the former creates an inverse record and passes collaboration gates.
implications.rationale: The Git and GitHub patterns preserve provenance, review, and merge semantics instead of silently moving a shared pointer.

implications.implication: Represent every recovery operation with an operation_id, operation_kind, target_state_id, parent_state_id, actor or request identity, artifact manifest, provenance, reversibility, coverage, and retention metadata.
implications.rationale: The reviewed products expose different target identifiers and durability boundaries; a common envelope makes those differences explicit and auditable.

implications.implication: Require a preflight preview for multi-artifact or shared-history recovery showing target identity, before and after state, added or modified or deleted artifacts, diff or line counts, and current-state freshness.
implications.rationale: Diff-driven inspection and confirmation are documented patterns, and freshness is needed to avoid applying a stale target over newer work.

implications.implication: Make destructive reset or rewind confirmation proportional to risk: state the exact verb, scope, non-captured changes, reversibility guarantee, and available escape path, with accessible text and a cancel action.
implications.rationale: Git documents destructive modes and agent products document coverage limits; WCAG supplies reversible, checked, or confirmed error-prevention alternatives.

implications.implication: Separate artifact restore from conversation or plan restore and offer code-only, conversation-only, both, and forked alternate recovery where the product state supports it.
implications.rationale: Independent state scopes prevent users from losing reasoning context when they only meant to restore artifacts, or vice versa.

implications.implication: Model partial failure and concurrency as first-class recovery states with conflict artifacts, continue or skip or abort actions, safe retry boundaries, and post-recovery verification.
implications.rationale: Git exposes continuation and abort states, while checkpoint storage and concurrent edits make an unconditional binary success unsafe.

implications.implication: Emit an auditable recovery event for local restores and preserve the original source and target provenance; shared reverts should remain visible as new changes.
implications.rationale: Recovery is itself a state transition and should be reversible or explainable even when the underlying file restore is local.

implications.implication: No current research evidence establishes which Puppet Master artifact classes or external side effects are transactionally recoverable; the product contract must decide this before promising full rewind.
implications.rationale: The reviewed sources do not define a general inverse for arbitrary external effects, so unsupported recovery scope must remain explicit.

novel_ideas.idea: Adopt a recovery preview card that combines target checkpoint, request or commit identity, operation semantics, affected-artifact counts and diff, retention or durability, and the exact post-action state before confirmation.
novel_ideas.rationale: The components are documented independently in mature tools; combining them into one operation preview reduces ambiguity at the decision point.

novel_ideas.idea: Add a per-artifact recovery coverage badge with captured, partially captured, or not captured states and reasons such as Bash, external, concurrent, or retention boundaries.
novel_ideas.rationale: Coverage is a documented limitation and storage is a documented trust and durability choice; surfacing both per artifact turns hidden gaps into actionable UX.

novel_ideas.idea: Use a dual-axis rewind control: independently select artifact state and conversation or plan state, then choose restore, fork, or keep current for each axis.
novel_ideas.rationale: The separate code and conversation choices documented by VS Code and Claude can be made more legible as independent state axes rather than hidden menu branches.

novel_ideas.idea: Before a destructive reset, create a named short-lived escape checkpoint with a visible operation ID, expiry, and reflog or ORIG_HEAD-style recovery route.
novel_ideas.rationale: Git already records ORIG_HEAD and reflog breadcrumbs for some local operations, while agent tools use checkpoints; a deliberately named escape state can make destructive recovery less opaque.

novel_ideas.idea: Use an optimistic concurrency guard: apply a recovery only when the current workspace fingerprint still matches the preview, otherwise block and show the changed artifacts before recomputing the target.
novel_ideas.rationale: The sources expose checkpoint scope and non-captured concurrent changes but do not define a universal guard; a freshness check directly addresses that gap.

novel_ideas.idea: Treat portable semantic rollback of arbitrary external side effects such as network calls, deployments, or database mutations as an explicitly unproven recovery mode rather than a default rewind capability.
novel_ideas.rationale: No reviewed source establishes a safe generic inverse for those effects; the idea is a boundary for future research, not a feature claim.

unresolved_questions.question: The reviewed products expose commit or ref IDs, local-history revisions, timestamps, prompt IDs, and checkpoint UUIDs; what canonical recovery ID should Puppet Master use to link the operation, artifact snapshot, and later inverse?
When a recovery preview becomes stale because of concurrent edits, should Puppet Master block, merge, create a conflict branch, or require the user to select a newly recomputed target?
What retention and durability guarantee is required for recovery records after session expiration, workspace deletion, repository garbage collection, or migration between machines?
Which operations may be retried after partial failure, and which commands or external side effects must be marked non-retryable or compensating-only?
Should every restore create a new audit event and optional inverse checkpoint so that the recovery itself can be undone without relying on an opaque local undo stack?

Which accessibility requirements beyond reversible, checked, or confirmed apply to the desktop or native presentation of recovery diffs, status announcements, focus order, and destructive confirmations?
